newsitem.title: FRANCE: French "hot autumn" cool despite strike calls.
newsitem.headline: French "hot autumn" cool despite strike calls.

text.p: It may look like deja vu, but the announcement of one-day strikes by France's teachers' and civil service trade unions do not necessarily herald a wave of labour unrest on last year's massive scale.

Seven unions have called a day of strikes and action on October 17 to fight the planned axing of 6,000 civil service jobs and to demand the opening of pay negotiations. Teachers have set a 24-hour strike on the same issues for next Monday.
Yet, while opinion polls show the centre-right government is deeply unpopular and the public mood gloomily angry, there are few signs of mass mobiisation so far.

The Force Ouvriere (FO) union, which spearheaded a crippling 24-day public transport strike last November and December, drew a far smaller than expected crowd at a national protest rally in Paris on Saturday, and the turnout in other stoppages and demonstrations this month has disappointed the organisers.
Ever since July, union leaders and opposition politicians have been threatening a "hot autumn" of strikes over budget austerity, record 12.5 percent unemployment and job cuts.
So far it has been distinctly cool.

"One cannot talk of an old-fashioned hot autumn but the gulf is widening between anxious, pent-up workers, bosses who take no time to think and politicians incapable of making sense of the way society is developing," Jacques Bouchaud, vice-chairman of the National Association of Personnel Managers, said.
"I fear an implosion rather than an explosion, but it's no less serious," he told the newspaper Le Monde.

The announcement of a 1997 budget freezing public spending at this year's level -- a 1.2 percent real cut -- with income tax cuts for the better-off offset by hikes in other taxes that hit everyone has compounded the government's unpopularity.

An opinion poll published on Sunday showed President Jacques Chirac's public approval rating had fallen by seven points to a mere 31 percent in a month, and Prime Minister Alain Juppe's by four points to only 27 percent.

Yet analysts say there has not yet been the single spark to ignite a labour revolt equivalent to last year's rebellion over Juppe's plan to curb welfare spending and streamline the loss-making state railways.

The government has been careful to avoid alienating rail and public transport workers, and Juppe has said he does not plan to extend a freeze on non-built-in civil service pay rises, promising wage negotiations in due course.
The unions are as busy fighting each other for control of the management of the state unemployment insurance fund, a major source of patronage, as they are in fighting the government.

And since the French employers' federation has the casting vote in deciding whether FO, the Socialist-led CFDT or the white-collar CGC wins that battle, the unions are not looking to alienate the bosses before the October 1 decision.
The workers' response to planned layoffs in the armaments industry, banks and aerospace has been feeble so far.
Even Louis Viannet, general secretary of the traditionally militant Communist-led CGT union, is cautious in his forecast.

"I keep hearing "things are going to explode this autumn'. I really don't know, but we are in a situation which could very rapidly trigger a reflex of revolt." he told Le Monde in an interview last week.

FO leader Marc Blondel had billed last Saturday's rally as a "springboard" for further action and a mobilisation test. Only 12,000 demonstrators showed up, according to police and up to double that according to the union -- compared to the 100,000 Blondel had predicted.
